sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: So the question the saga pattern answers is the pragmatic one: **when a single ACID transaction is impossible, what is the smallest change to the problem that makes a single business outcome possible?** The answer: break the business transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each of which *can* be undone, and accept that "undo" is itself a local transaction.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The pattern was first formalized by Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem in their 1987 paper *Sagas*, in the context of long-running database transactions.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Where the Bulkhead pattern isolates failure by partitioning resources into separate pools, the Saga pattern coordinates recovery across services that no longer share a single database.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: A saga is, formally, a sequence of **local transactions** $T_1 \to T_2 \to \cdots \to T_n$, each paired with a **compensating transaction** $C_i$.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Forward progress happens left-to-right; on the first failure, the saga runs the compensations in reverse for every $T_i$ that already completed.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The compensating $C_i$ is a real action — CancelFlight , RefundPayment , ReleaseSeat — not a database rollback.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Sagas coordinate what database transactions cannot.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: This post covers the two top-level variants — **orchestration** (a central coordinator tells each service what to do) and **choreography** (each service reacts to events on a wire) — plus three implementation shapes, a trade-off section, and a decision matrix.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The related-patterns section at the end points forward to **Circuit Breaker** and the **Outbox Pattern** — the patterns every non-trivial saga turns out to need.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Same shape, two logics of control.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Orchestrated saga.** A single service — the *orchestrator* — knows the saga's steps.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: It calls flight.reserve , then hotel.reserve , then car.reserve , in order.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Each step returns success or failure to the orchestrator, which decides the next move.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: On any failure, the orchestrator emits the compensating calls in reverse order to the steps that already completed.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The orchestrator persists a **saga log**: a per-saga append-only journal of which steps have completed and which have been compensated, so a crash can be recovered by replaying the journal.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Choreographed saga.** There is no orchestrator.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Each service emits events on a message broker ( FlightReserved , HotelReserved ) and listens for events from the other services.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The saga's forward progress is the path events follow through the system; compensations are services that listen for TripBookingFailed and react.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The state of the saga lives in the broker's offsets and each participant's local store.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: There is no single log; each participant owns its own slice.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The monolith is fine.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The microservices version is what happens when the monolith has been split for good reasons — independent deploys, team boundaries, scaling policies.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The saga is not a worse transaction; it is a different shape of work, with different failure modes and a different operational surface.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The orchestrator is the **single owner of the saga's state**.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Every step, every compensation, every retry, every timeout is its concern.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The participant services know nothing of the broader saga — flight.reserve is the same call it would receive from any caller.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: This decoupling from the participant side is the orchestrator's virtue.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: No central service owns anything.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The saga's forward progress is whatever sequence of events the broker delivers.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The compensation flow is *another* sequence of events, going the other way.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The brittleness is hidden in the cross-service event contracts: a TripBookingRequested event changes schema, and three downstream consumers need to be migrated in lock-step.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: :::tip{title="The 'who owns the saga?' question is the right test"}↵Orchestrated sagas are owned by the orchestrator.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Choreographed sagas are owned by *every consumer that handles a related event* — by the time the team's fully drawn, the "owner" is whichever engineer happens to be awake when the broker goes down.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Pick the variant whose ownership story you can sustain at 3 a.m.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The pattern's name implies forward progress.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The actual work is *backward progress on demand*.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: For every forward transaction $T_i$, the saga must define a compensating transaction $C_i$ that semantically undoes $T_i$ — not a database rollback, an action.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: In the canonical microservices.io travel-booking example, the saga is:

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: | Step | Forward ($T_i$) | Compensation ($C_i$) |↵|------|-----------------|----------------------|↵| 1 | ReserveFlight | CancelFlightReservation |↵| 2 | ReserveHotel | CancelHotelReservation |↵| 3 | ReserveCar | CancelCarReservation |↵| 4 | ReserveAirportTransfer | CancelAirportTransfer |↵| 5 | ActivateTravelInsurance | CancelTravelInsurance |

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The compensations are not DELETE FROM booking WHERE id = ?

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices
The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: They are **business actions** that undo the business effect of the forward step: cancel the booking with the airline's API, release the room back to the hotel's inventory, mark the car available again.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: A compensation can itself fail — which is the saga's most-overlooked failure mode.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Imagine CancelFlightReservation itself fails.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The airline's API returns 503 just as the saga is trying to clean up.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Now the saga is stuck in a half-compensated state: the flight reservation is still live in the airline's system (money committed), the hotel and car are cancelled (good), and the orchestrator (or choreographed consumer) is looping on the compensation.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The patterns that address this are:

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Idempotent compensations.** Every compensation carries an idempotency_key derived from (saga_id, step_id, "compensation") .

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The first call has effect; subsequent retries with the same key are no-ops.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The compensation's effect is the same whether it succeeds on the first call or the hundred-and-first.↵**Retry-with-backoff at the saga level.** The orchestrator (or the choreographed consumer) retries the failed compensation on a schedule — exponential backoff capped at a maximum interval, repeating until the compensation succeeds or a human-driven timeout aborts the saga.↵**A saga log for the saga.** When even the compensation log is unreliable, escalate to a *meta-saga* that monitors the primary saga's stuck compensations and applies operational interventions (manual credit, partial refund), surfacing them to a human operator for the cases automation cannot resolve.↵**Idempotency at the participant.** The participant service is the last line of defence: if it receives CancelFlightReservation twice with the same idempotency key, the second call is a no-op.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Sagas cannot work without participant-level idempotency.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: :::anote{title="The forward step that has no compensation is a design smell"}↵If you find a forward step in your saga that has no clean compensation, the step probably does not belong in the saga — the failure mode for "we cannot undo this" is not "compensate harder," it is "do not perform the irreversible action until irreversibility is no longer a problem." Real-world example: an ActivateInsurancePolicy step has a compensation ( CancelPolicy ) but only if activation has a pending window.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Past the window, there is no compensation.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The fix is to keep activation inside a managed-delay state machine, not to write a clever saga around the irreversible case.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The partial-compensation edge case — refund minus a cancellation fee, partial reversal, side-effect-irreversible steps — is a rich topic of its own, with failure modes that do not fit cleanly into the "full undo" model above.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **A follow-up post in this series will cover compensation semantics in depth** — see the related-patterns section at the end for the slot.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The model's full-undo assumption is the load-bearing one for understanding saga implementation today; partial compensations are a strict superset that require a richer state model.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The pattern is shape, not product.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The three shapes below are what you will see in production code — Temporal, Camunda, AWS Step Functions all live under the third shape; the first two are hand-rolled.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The simplest production-ready implementation is an orchestrator service that runs the saga's step graph against real participant services.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The saga log is a table in the orchestrator's database.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Step failures trigger backward-running compensations.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The shape is: a step iterator, a retry/backoff loop per step, a compensation loop driven by the saga log, and a state machine on the log itself.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: A real implementation moves log into a database row with optimistic concurrency; this code is the conceptual scaffold, not the production file.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Add saga-log-persistence, error-out to a dead-letter queue, and a meta-saga for stuck compensations, and you have a hand-rolled orchestrator that ships.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The choreography shape is *no orchestrator*.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Each participant service owns its slice of the saga and reacts to events on a message broker.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The state of the saga is distributed.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The load-bearing shape here is: **events flow forward, then compensation events flow backward**.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Each consumer has its own idempotency story.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The "saga state" is whatever any one consumer can derive from the events it has seen; there is no global view.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The ergonomic cost of choreography shows up exactly here: every participant has to know which events to react to and which to ignore, and any new step in the saga requires changing every other consumer's logic.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The orchestrator expresses this as a list; choreography expresses it as a graph.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: A workflow engine externalizes the orchestrator.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The engine persists the saga log, schedules retries, and offers observability for running sagas out of the box.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The team writes the saga's logic; the engine runs it.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: This is the same shape as Shape 1, but the orchestrator's "saga log" is the Temporal state store, the "retry" is the activity retry policy, and the "compensation" is the workflow's catch block.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Production teams reach for engines when the hand-rolled version's failure modes (saga-log persistence, observability, long-running sagas that survive deploys) start costing more than the engine itself.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: | Shape | When to reach for it | Trade-off |↵|-------|----------------------|-----------|↵| Hand-rolled orchestrator | You have one team, simple workflows, and want to read every line of the saga code itself | You own the saga-log persistence, observability, and recovery story |↵| Choreography | Participants are owned by separate teams; the saga is loosely-coupled by design | Observability cost; cross-team event-schema coordination |↵| Workflow engine | Long-running sagas (minutes to days), high cardinality of saga variants, need durable execution that survives deploys | Adds a vendor / self-host dependency; engine-specific concepts |

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The saga pattern is not free.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Three trade-offs and three observability surfaces.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Operational complexity.** A saga has three things to monitor per step (forward success, compensation success, stuck-compensation), a retry policy per step, and a saga log that has to survive process restarts and database migrations.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: A monolith has a transaction; a saga has an operating procedure.↵**Eventual consistency window.** Between the moment a saga's forward step succeeds and the moment every downstream service sees the resulting state, the saga is *inconsistent*.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The window can be milliseconds (synchronous orchestrator, fast broker) or minutes (choreography, manual interventions).

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The business has to reason about queries that span the window — *"is the flight booked?"* has a different answer depending on whether the hotel service has seen the saga yet.↵**Coupling trade-off.** Orchestration couples the *orchestrator* to every participant's contract; choreography couples *every participant* to every other participant's event schemas.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Pick which side of that trade you want to be on.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The three surfaces that make or break a saga in production:

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Idempotency keys per step.** Every forward call and every compensation carries idempotency_key = hash(saga_id, step_id, "compensation"|"forward") .

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Search by idempotency key shows the full saga state, even if the saga log is partial.↵**Correlation IDs.** Every log line, trace, and metric for a saga step carries saga_id and trace_id .

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: A single query should be able to reconstruct the saga's history from logs and traces alone, without consulting the saga log.↵**Saga-state dashboards.** Count sagas by state ( started , forward , compensating , completed , failed , stuck ) over time.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Stuck-compensations are the most important metric — they are the ones that need a human.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: :::success{title="If you cannot see stuck-saga-state count in your monitoring, you do not have saga observability"}↵A saga log that is not exposed to a runbook is invisible.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The simplest dashboard is two counters: forward-progress ( started → completed over the last hour) and compensation-progress ( compensating → compensated over the last hour).

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: When the second number spikes, you have a problem; when the first number plateaus, you have a worse one.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Reach for the variant whose shape fits the problem.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Eight rules, each one a test.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: :::anote{title="Decision Matrix — orchestration vs choreography, eight rules" icon="🧭"}

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 1 — Reach for orchestration when the saga's logic is owned by one team.**↵If a single team owns the workflow's steps *and* every participant service, an orchestrator expresses the saga as a list and the team can read it.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The coupling cost is local; the observability is one place.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 2 — Reach for choreography when participants are owned by many teams.**↵If the flight service, the hotel service, and the car service are owned by separate teams with separate deploy cadences, no orchestrator belongs to any one of them.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The choreography's event contracts are the only honest API surface.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 3 — Reach for orchestration when the saga's state must be globally observable.**↵If you need to answer *"how many sagas are stuck compensating right now?"* with one dashboard query, orchestration's saga log gives you that for free.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Choreography gives you a distributed assembly problem.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 4 — Reach for choreography when the saga has no natural "director" service.**↵Some sagas have no obvious orchestrator candidate — adding one is a service you would have to write and operate.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Choreography is cheaper to start and lets the participants evolve independently.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 5 — Reach for a workflow engine when sagas run for hours or days.**↵Hand-rolled orchestrators do not survive deploys well.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Engines (Temporal, Camunda, Step Functions) persist the saga log through deploys, cluster failures, and operator mistakes; the engine cost is paid back in incidents you do not have.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 6 — Reach for choreography only if your events carry full state.**↵A choreographed saga's FlightReserved event needs enough information for the hotel service to do its work *without calling back to the flight service*.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Choreography with chatty callbacks is orchestration in disguise, and worse.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 7 — Reach for orchestration when compensations are common.**↵If the compensation path runs more than the forward path in production, the cost of "every consumer reacts to events" becomes a tax on every change.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Orchestration makes the compensation path a single function call.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 8 — Reach for choreography when the team has invested in event-sourcing.**↵Choreography is *natural* on top of an event-sourced system, where every state change is already an event and every consumer reads from the same log.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Choreography on top of stateful databases without events is awkward and slow.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: **Rule 0 (load-bearing) — Reach for neither when a single ACID transaction fits.**↵If all five legs of the booking can live in one database with one connection, the saga is over-engineering.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Sagas buy you a capability; do not pay for it when you do not need it.↵:::

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: Read it once, save it in the team's wiki, and the next saga feature you scope will find its variant on the first read.

sourceRef.title: The Saga Pattern: Coordinating Long-Lived Transactions Across Microservices

sentences.text: The two variants — orchestration and choreography — are the same shape with two logics of control: one says "do this, then this, then this"; the other says "react to this, then react to that." Both carry the same load: forward transactions paired with compensations, persisted in a saga log you can recover from, observable through correlation IDs and stuck-saga counters, and fronted by a decision procedure that picks the variant whose shape matches your constraints.

sentences.text: ↵A workshop has three things in it: a craftsman, a workbench, and an apprenticeship notebook.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The craftsman is the model.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Fast, general-purpose, capable of turning raw text into plans, code, and prose — but, on his own, he is only as good as his training.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Give him a problem he has never seen and he will improvise, which is a polite way of saying he will guess.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The workbench is **MCP**.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Power tools bolted down to the bench — a drill, a bandsaw, a calculator, a live wire to GitHub, a connection to your database.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Each tool does one thing.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Each tool is discoverable by name, has a typed input, and produces a typed output.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The craftsman reaches for a tool when he needs to act on the world: query the database, fetch the file, send the email, run the calculation.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The workbench is the *outside* — live, stateful, replaceable.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Swap the bench for a different one and the craftsman can do a different kind of work without changing who he is.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The apprenticeship notebook is **Agent Skills**.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The notes left by every master who has worked at this bench before — the house style guide, the recipe for filling out a PDF form, the multi-step procedure for posting a code review, the company-specific way of writing a commit message.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The notebook is read on demand.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The craftsman does not memorise every page; he opens the right chapter when the task matches.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The notebook is the *inside* — codified, version-controlled, shareable across craftsman after craftsman.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Now imagine the three failure modes.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: **Failure mode 1: craftsman with a full workbench, no notebook.** He has the drill but no idea which drill bit to use, or that he should *measure twice before drilling once*.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: He hammers when he should screw.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: He calls gh list_prs seventeen times in a row because he has no procedure for "this is what a code review looks like at our company." Powerful, dangerous, expensive.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: **Failure mode 2: craftsman with a thick notebook, no workbench.** He knows every procedure in the book — fill out a form, post a review, write a release note — but every procedure ends with *"then call the gh API."* And he has no gh API.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: He writes beautiful prose about what he would do if he had tools.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Helpful in theory, impotent in practice.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: **Failure mode 3: craftsman with neither.** A bare LLM.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: He can pattern-match and improvise.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Some of the time, that is enough.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Most of the time, the improvisation is wrong in ways you cannot detect, because — as last month's post on sycophancy spent three thousand words explaining — the model agrees with whatever shape of question you ask it, and the shape of the question is the entire signal it has.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The interesting design space is the craftsman with **both**.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: That is the modern agent stack: a model, an MCP workbench full of typed tools, and a Skills notebook full of codified procedure, composing in real time.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: This post is about why those two systems — MCP and Skills — are not rivals, how they actually differ under the hood, and a decision procedure for reaching for one, the other, or both.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: :::anote{title="A 30-second preview, in two screenshots" icon="🔧"}↵**MCP** is a *runtime protocol*.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The model discovers tools by sending tools/list over JSON-RPC.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: It calls a tool by sending tools/call with a JSON payload that matches the tool's schema.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The server runs the tool and returns a typed result.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: The round trip is hundreds of milliseconds.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Tools are *executable*.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: **Skills** is a *folder format*.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: A directory with a SKILL.md whose YAML frontmatter has name and description .

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: At agent startup, every skill's name and description are loaded into the system prompt.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: When a task matches a description, the agent reads the full SKILL.md into context and may also execute bundled scripts.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: No network round trip — the skill is on disk.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Skills are *codified*.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: If MCP is the workbench, Skills is the notebook — and the notebook now ships tools under scripts/ as well as recipes under SKILL.md .

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Different shapes of information.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Different latency profiles.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Different failure modes.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Same agent.↵:::

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Both standards have a single letter in their names that does a lot of work: **S**.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: *Server* in MCP, *Skills* in Agent Skills.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: Both are described as ways to "extend what an LLM can do." Both are supported by Claude, by VS Code, by Cursor, by a growing list of AI clients.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals

sentences.text: A reasonable engineer, on a Tuesday morning, scrolling through release notes, will read "MCP server" and "Agent Skill" and conclude that they are two competing ways to solve the same problem.

sourceRef.title: Workbench and Notebook: Why MCP Servers and Agent Skills Are Not Rivals
